bibl.title: Machine Learning in Agriculture: A Review

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: published applications of machine learning in agricultural production - crop, livestock, water and soil management - and the ML models they used
span.quote: The works analyzed were categorized in (a) crop management, including applications on yield prediction, disease detection, weed detection crop quality, and species recognition; (b) livestock management, including applications on animal welfare and livestock production; (c) water management; and (d) soil management.

span.label: which machine learning models have been applied to which agricultural problems, and in what proportions
span.quote: In this paper, we present a comprehensive review of research dedicated to applications of machine learning in agricultural production systems.

span.label: a four-way classification of ML applications in agriculture over 40 journal articles, with the model-by-subcategory distribution, prefaced by a plain statement of ML terminology
span.quote: The reviewed articles have been, on a first level, classified in four generic categories; namely, crop management, livestock management, water management, and soil management.

span.label: existence
span.quote: From the above figures and tables, we show that ML models have been applied in multiple applications for crop management (61%); mostly yield prediction (20%) and disease detection (22%).

span.label: sensor-generated agricultural data outrunning the analytical methods available to act on it
span.quote: By applying machine learning to sensor data, farm management systems are evolving into real time artificial intelligence enabled programs that provide rich recommendations and insights for farmer decision support and action.

span.label: a narrative review of 40 journal articles found through Scopus, ScienceDirect and PubMed, covering 2004 onward, classified into four management categories
span.term: a narrative review of 40 journal articles found through Scopus, ScienceDirect and PubMed, covering 2004 onward, classified into four management categories
span.quote: The search engines implemented were Scopus, ScienceDirect and PubMed. The selected articles regard works presented solely in journal papers.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE LEARNING SIGNAL IS WHAT DIVIDES THE TWO FAMILIES: supervised learning has inputs paired with outputs and builds a mapping; unsupervised has no train/test distinction at all and looks for hidden structure. The difference is in what the data carries, not in the algorithm chosen
span.quote: In unsupervised learning, however, there is no distinction between training and test sets with data being unlabeled. The learner processes input data with the goal of discovering hidden patterns.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION RUNS BEFORE THE MODEL, IN BOTH FAMILIES, to give a lower-dimensional representation preserving as much information as possible - and it is applied specifically to avoid the effects of dimensionality rather than as a modelling choice
span.quote: It is usually performed prior to applying a classification or regression model in order to avoid the effects of dimensionality.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: CROP APPLICATIONS DOMINATE BECAUSE THEIR DATA NEEDS NO FUSION: ML predictions in crop management can be extracted from images alone, whereas livestock, water and soil work requires combining recorded data sources - so the distribution reflects DATA ASSEMBLY COST rather than the difficulty of the ML
span.quote: In contrast, when data recordings are involved, occasionally at the level of big data, the implementations of ML are less in number, mainly because of the increased efforts required for the data analysis task and not for the ML models per se.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE APPROACHES ARE NOT WIRED INTO DECISIONS: every reviewed application is an individual solution not adequately connected with the decision-making process, which is the paper's own account of why the field has not consolidated
span.quote: At the moment, all of the approaches regard individual approaches and solutions and are not adequately connected with the decision-making process, as seen in other application domains.

span.label: NO INCLUSION CRITERIA ARE GIVEN. Three search engines are named and 40 articles are reported, with no keywords, no screening rule and no count of what was excluded - so the percentages describe a corpus assembled by unstated means
span.quote: The search engines implemented were Scopus, ScienceDirect and PubMed. The selected articles regard works presented solely in journal papers.

span.label: journal papers only, which excludes the conference literature where much applied ML appears
span.quote: The search engines implemented were Scopus, ScienceDirect and PubMed. The selected articles regard works presented solely in journal papers.

span.label: climate prediction is excluded by declaration rather than by a criterion, on the ground that it is a complete area by itself
span.quote: Climate prediction, although very important for agricultural production, has not been included in the presented review, considering the fact that ML applications for climate prediction is a complete area by itself.

span.label: the ML models described are only those implemented in the reviewed works, so the terminology section is bounded by the sample rather than by the field
span.quote: The presentation of the learning models in ML is limited to the ones that have been implemented in works presented in this review.

span.label: 25 of the 40 articles come from a single journal, Computers and Electronics in Agriculture, and six more from one other - so the sample is concentrated in two venues
span.quote: Twenty-five (25) of the presented articles were published in the journal «Computer and Electronics in Agriculture», six were published in the journal of «Biosystems Engineering»

span.label: the authors state that all reviewed approaches are individual solutions not adequately connected with the decision-making process
span.quote: At the moment, all of the approaches regard individual approaches and solutions and are not adequately connected with the decision-making process, as seen in other application domains.

span.label: the scope is bounded and stated: three named search engines, journal papers only, 2004 onward, and climate prediction excluded by declaration
span.note: eliminates: an unbounded reading of the review's percentages - the scope is stated: three search engines, journal papers only, 2004 onward, climate prediction excluded. It does not eliminate selection bias, because no inclusion criteria are given · outcome: partial
span.quote: The search engines implemented were Scopus, ScienceDirect and PubMed. The selected articles regard works presented solely in journal papers.

span.label: the presentation of learning models is limited to those actually implemented in the reviewed works, rather than a general survey of ML
span.note: eliminates: the terminology section being read as a survey of machine learning as a field - it is declared limited to the models actually implemented in the reviewed works · outcome: held
span.quote: The presentation of the learning models in ML is limited to the ones that have been implemented in works presented in this review.

span.label: machine learning
span.quote: In this paper, we present a comprehensive review of research dedicated to applications of machine learning in agricultural production systems.

span.label: training data
span.quote: Typically, ML methodologies involves a learning process with the objective to learn from “experience” (training data) to perform a task.

span.label: features
span.quote: Usually, an individual example is described by a set of attributes, also known as features or variables.

span.label: attributes
span.quote: Usually, an individual example is described by a set of attributes, also known as features or variables.

span.label: performance metric
span.quote: The performance of the ML model in a specific task is measured by a performance metric that is improved with experience over time.

span.label: supervised learning
span.quote: In supervised learning, data are presented with example inputs and the corresponding outputs, and the objective is to construct a general rule that maps inputs to outputs.

span.label: unsupervised learning
span.quote: In unsupervised learning, however, there is no distinction between training and test sets with data being unlabeled. The learner processes input data with the goal of discovering hidden patterns.

span.label: reinforcement learning
span.quote: In some cases, inputs can be only partially available with some of the target outputs missing or given only as feedback to the actions in a dynamic environment (reinforcement learning).

span.label: Dimensionality reduction
span.quote: Dimensionality reduction (DR) is an analysis that is executed in both families of supervised and unsupervised learning types, with the aim of providing a more compact, lower-dimensional representation of a dataset to preserve as much information as possible from the original data.

span.label: principal component analysis
span.quote: Some of the most common DR algorithms are the following: (i) principal component analysis \ [22\], (ii) partial least squares regression \ [23\], and (iii) linear discriminant analysis

span.label: linear discriminant analysis
span.quote: Some of the most common DR algorithms are the following: (i) principal component analysis \ [22\], (ii) partial least squares regression \ [23\], and (iii) linear discriminant analysis

span.label: crop management
span.quote: The works analyzed were categorized in (a) crop management, including applications on yield prediction, disease detection, weed detection crop quality, and species recognition; (b) livestock management, including applications on animal welfare and livestock production; (c) water management; and (d) soil management.

span.label: feature - THREE NAMES FOR ONE THING, SAID IN ONE SENTENCE: `a set of attributes, ALSO KNOWN AS features or variables`. The corpus holds `variables` as a content_tags layer and `features` as a concept on other records, and this is the paper that says they are the same object seen from statistics, from machine learning and from experimental design
span.quote: Usually, an individual example is described by a set of attributes, also known as features or variables.

span.label: supervised / unsupervised - THE DIVIDING LINE IS THE LEARNING SIGNAL, NOT THE ALGORITHM. Supervised means inputs arrive with their outputs and the goal is a rule mapping one to the other; unsupervised means there is NO DISTINCTION BETWEEN TRAINING AND TEST SETS at all, which is a stronger statement than `unlabelled data` and is what makes the two families incomparable on accuracy
span.quote: In unsupervised learning, however, there is no distinction between training and test sets with data being unlabeled. The learner processes input data with the goal of discovering hidden patterns.

span.label: reinforcement learning - PLACED HERE AS A PARTIAL CASE OF SUPERVISION rather than a third family: inputs partially available, some target outputs missing or given only as feedback to actions in a dynamic environment. Other papers in this corpus treat it as a peer of the other two, and the disagreement is about what the taxonomy is FOR
span.quote: In some cases, inputs can be only partially available with some of the target outputs missing or given only as feedback to the actions in a dynamic environment (reinforcement learning).

span.label: this paper's `review` - A NARRATIVE REVIEW WITH A SEARCH ENGINE LIST AND NO INCLUSION CRITERIA. Scopus, ScienceDirect and PubMed are named; no keywords, no screening rule and no exclusion count are given, and 40 is reported as a result. Its percentages are therefore descriptive of a corpus assembled by unstated means
span.quote: The search engines implemented were Scopus, ScienceDirect and PubMed. The selected articles regard works presented solely in journal papers.

span.label: distinguishes-from → ML applications to climate prediction, deliberately excluded from this review on the ground that it is a complete area by itself
span.quote: Climate prediction, although very important for agricultural production, has not been included in the presented review, considering the fact that ML applications for climate prediction is a complete area by itself.

span.label: attributes —same-as→ features
span.quote: Usually, an individual example is described by a set of attributes, also known as features or variables.

span.label: supervised learning —distinct-from→ unsupervised learning
span.quote: In supervised learning, data are presented with example inputs and the corresponding outputs, and the objective is to construct a general rule that maps inputs to outputs. In some cases, inputs can be only partially available with some of the target outputs missing or given only as feedback to the actions in a dynamic environment (reinforcement learning). In the supervised setting, the acquired expertise (trained model) is used to predict the missing outputs (labels) for the test data. In unsupervised learning, however, there is no distinction between training and test sets with data being unlabeled. The learner processes input data with the goal of discovering hidden patterns.

span.label: Dimensionality reduction —operationalised-as→ principal component analysis
span.quote: Some of the most common DR algorithms are the following: (i) principal component analysis \ [22\], (ii) partial least squares regression \ [23\], and (iii) linear discriminant analysis

span.label: performance metric —operationalised-as→ machine learning
span.quote: The performance of the ML model in a specific task is measured by a performance metric that is improved with experience over time.

span.label: crop management accounts for 61% of the reviewed ML applications, mostly yield prediction (20%) and disease detection (22%)
span.quote: From the above figures and tables, we show that ML models have been applied in multiple applications for crop management (61%); mostly yield prediction (20%) and disease detection (22%).

span.label: ANNs and SVMs dominate - ANNs in crop, water and soil management, SVMs in livestock
span.quote: It is also evident from the analysis that most of the studies used ANN and SVM ML models. More specifically, ANNs were used mostly for implementations in crop, water, and soil management, while SVMs were used mostly for livestock management.

span.label: livestock, water and soil applications are roughly equal at 19%, 10% and 10%, which the authors attribute to the cost of assembling recorded data rather than to the ML
span.quote: This fact partially explains the almost equal distribution of ML applications in livestock management (19%), water management (10%), and soil management (10%).

span.label: eight ML models were found across the 40 articles
span.quote: From the analysis of these articles, it was found that eight ML models have been implemented in total.
